#5639. Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

Testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.

Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns

To investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

Between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

The researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

Men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein showed the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.

Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links

A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.

Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

Meat protein showed a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.

These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

Despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

"Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," says Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

An important limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.

#5638. Opinion: More surgeons in Africa isn’t enough when only 10% are women

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Vadset is a research collaborator at Harvard Medical School’s Program in Global Surgery and Social Change and a fourth-year medical student at Albert Einstein College of Medicine.

A voice cuts through the commotion of the Kigali operating room — calm and resolute, directing the staff as they prep the patient. Standing at the head of the table is Dr. Françoise Mukagaju, the first female plastic surgeon in Rwanda. Beside her is Dr. Victoire Mukamitari, the soon-to-be second.

I watched this film from a theater in New York, half a world away, during the 81st United Nations General Assembly, a week filled with speeches about human capital and health systems built to last. “The Making of a Surgeon” follows Mukamitari through the operating room, as well as her training, her family, and the expectations of both. I saw what the week’s speeches kept missing: Global surgery cannot grow its workforce without women, yet the systems built to grow it are not required to measure them.

A recent analysis of the surgeon workforce in 12 of the 14 member countries of the College of Surgeons of East, Central and Southern Africa (COSECSA) found that women make up one-tenth of the surgical workforce. This number has gone unchanged since 2015 despite a 42% increase in the total number of surgeons in the region. Meanwhile, 5 billion people worldwide lack access to safe and affordable surgical care.

I was 15 when a friend’s mother told me I would never be a surgeon. Fortunately, I live where many female surgeons have paved the way for hopeful women and young girls — a luxury many across the globe do not have. (In the U.S., about 30% of surgeons are female.) One international study of women surgeons found that 56.4% had been told they could not be a surgeon because of their gender.

When the film’s moderator asked Mukagaju how she earned the respect of her male colleagues, her answer was simple: be excellent, and the respect will follow. Excellence is worth striving for. But that answer carries a quiet condition: that a woman must first prove herself exceptional before she is afforded the same respect and opportunity as her male colleagues. More importantly, though, excellence cannot be demonstrated without opportunity. Before a woman can prove that she belongs at the table, someone has to consider her, so perhaps the question is not simply, “How can women earn a seat at the table?” but rather, “How do we make sure women are given the opportunity to take one?”

But you cannot widen the door you refuse to measure. When the Lancet Commission on Global Surgery set its six global indicators for measuring surgical systems, specialist surgeon, anesthesiologist, and obstetrician density was defined, but with no breakdown by sex. A gap that goes unmeasured cannot be fixed, and what can’t be fixed won’t be funded. The vehicle to resolve this already exists: National Surgical, Obstetric, and Anesthesia Plans (NSOAPs), which serve in part as the platforms whose data drives funding decisions. Writing gender-disaggregated indicators into NSOAPs can bring visibility to this disparity. The method itself is not missing — only the decision to look.

Some will argue that gender equity in surgery is a soft target, and that the real crisis is the sheer shortage of surgeons. They’re half right: The shortage is the crisis. That same 42% growth in surgeons raised density by just 0.06 surgeons per 100,000 people. At that pace, the region will not train its way out of this gap by recruiting from the same narrow pool.

Women comprise roughly 40% of recent medical graduates in sub-Saharan Africa, yet they remain that same one-tenth of its surgeons because of barriers along the pipeline. Research suggests they’re discouraged from choosing surgery in medical school, harassed during residency, and face gendered assumptions and family pressures once they’re in practice. The low percentage of women among surgeons is not an aside to the workforce shortage. It is one of its causes. You cannot close the surgical gap while drawing surgeons almost entirely from the same narrow pool of men in each graduating class: mostly men.

The will is not absent. The Pan African Women’s Association of Surgeons connects women surgeons across the continent for mentorship, and regional colleges like COSECSA, among others, run their own initiatives. But mentorship networks and good intentions alone will not garner the money while the gap they address remains invisible in national plans.

Uplifting women in global surgery belongs in every one of these conversations, from NSOAPs to residency programs to the U.N. General Assembly. It is not the sole answer to a 5-billion-patient crisis. But it is a lever we can measure, fund, and act on now — and a promise to the women and girls who are still being told this work is not for them. More women standing at the operating table, like Mukagaju and Mukamitari, is how health systems are built to last.

Taylor Vadset is a research collaborator at Harvard Medical School’s Program in Global Surgery and Social Change and a fourth-year medical student at Albert Einstein College of Medicine.

#5637. Opinion: More doctors should prescribe exercise after a concussion

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Hamilton is founder of the Brain Care Catalyst Foundation.

Two decades ago, a Vespa accident put me in a coma. By the time I came home from acute rehab, I had lost 25 pounds, most of it muscle, and my left side did not work as it should. After months of hospital sponge baths, soaking in a warm bath until my fingers wrinkled was blissful — and then it was time to get out.

I couldn’t. At 40, I did not have the upper body strength to lift myself from the tub; I had to shout for my wife to help. The humiliation was clarifying. I needed a way back, and what I found was exercise.

It began gently, with an Ashtanga yoga instructor who came to the house a few times a week. At first even the warrior pose was a struggle, but week after week, the two sides of my body relearned how to work together, and before long, I could get out of the bathtub on my own.

Later, I traded downhill skiing for skate skiing, the technique biathletes use. With my lingering balance problems, I fell a dozen times or more in every lesson. But once I got the hang of it, the sport was exhilarating and punishing: thighs burning, heart rate high for an hour or more on the trails. One day I told my instructor, Jack Bellorado, a rugged former wilderness guide, that I’d had a great ski and only fallen three times. He looked at me and said, “You must not have been pushing yourself hard enough.”

Nearly everyone caring for me after the accident had been trying, sensibly, to keep me safe. Jack expected something hard of me. I needed both, and medical care for the millions of Americans who suffer challenging concussion symptoms months after their injury is still much better at the first than the second.

For years, the standard advice after a concussion was to rest in a dark room until symptoms passed. Newer research is moving away from that recommendation. In a 2019 randomized trial led by John Leddy at the University at Buffalo, 103 adolescents with sport-related concussions were divided into two groups. One was prescribed aerobic exercise and recovered in a median of 13 days, compared with 17 for those in the other group, who only stretched. In a small 2024 trial, people who had lived with moderate to severe brain injuries for six months or more walked farther and faster after a block of high-intensity training than after conventional rehabilitation. This small but important study needs to be replicated in larger trials and include people with concussions.

Medicine has learned of unhealthy overprotectiveness before. In the early 1950s, heart attack patients were kept flat in bed for weeks, because exertion was thought dangerous. Cardiologists Samuel Levine and Bernard Lown questioned whether prolonged bed rest was helping patients or harming them, and, over strong opposition, got them sitting up in armchairs. Their 1952 paper in JAMA helped start a long shift. Today, supervised exercise is a standard, reimbursed part of recovery after a heart attack. And cardiac care was not alone: over the past few decades, surgeons have moved from keeping patients flat for days to walking them within hours.

Brain injury has been slower to make this turn, in part because Hippocratic caution can turn into overprotection. To many medical professionals, it may seem risky to prescribe exercise. For patients, the injured organ is the one you think with, so trying to do as little as possible can seem wise. Exertion can briefly worsen headache, dizziness, and fog, which can feel like movement is doing harm. There is a grain of truth in the caution: The brain does much of its repair during sleep, so sleeping has a central place in recovery. But adequate sleep and daytime stillness are not the same thing, and the lesson from most other fields is that movement and rest are partners, not rivals.

Exercise may help the injured brain in three ways. The first is better sleep. Sleep problems are among the most common and stubborn complaints after brain injury, and exercise is associated with improved sleep. The second is that exercise alleviates depression, another common complication of TBI. The third is more speculative. Working muscles release lactate, far more of it during hard effort, and lactate can cross into the brain, where studies, mostly in animals, suggest it may help trigger production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, or BDNF, often called fertilizer for the brain. If sleep is when the brain does most of its repair work, a day’s exertion might help twice over: a better night’s rest, and more for the brain to work with during sleep. However likely, that remains unproven but worth testing.

Today I work with the TBI Post-Acute Care Clinic Collaborative. In conversations with clinicians, I repeatedly hear that exercise is rarely encouraged in brain-injury care and even less often formally prescribed. Patients may leave appointments with medications, referrals, and advice to stay active, but without an exercise prescription.

The evidence has limits. Results from adolescent athletes with concussion may not hold for adults with more severe injuries like mine, and such studies are scarce. Some people’s symptoms worsen with exertion. That is why care must be individualized, so patients don’t have to guess. Patients who want to use exercise to improve their recovery should have help determining what they can safely do: an assessment, a written plan with an intensity set for them, a path for progressing it, follow-up to adjust it, and supervision when they need it. Doctors can put this evidence into practice now, and insurers should cover clinically appropriate programs, as they do for cardiac or stroke rehabilitation.

In 1972, a pastor named Robert Perske wrote about tension in appropriate risk-taking. Perske, who led an association for people with intellectual disabilities in Omaha, Neb., was convinced that well-meaning overprotection was smothering the people it was meant to help. Decades before the rise of helicopter parenting, he wrote that “there can be such a thing as human dignity in risk” and “there can be a dehumanizing indignity in safety!” What people needed, he argued, was a “fair and prudent share of risk.”

Perske’s point was not that risk is good for its own sake. It was that a life arranged entirely around safety becomes a smaller life. I got out of that bathtub, and eventually onto those skinny skis, because people took care of me and pushed me. More patients recovering from brain injury should leave their appointments with an exercise prescription, with guardrails suited to their condition. The effort is theirs to make. The plan, and the support in following it, are ours to give.

Scott W. Hamilton is founder of the Brain Care Catalyst Foundation.

#5636. UnitedHealth the latest insurer to sue over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings

UnitedHealth the latest insurer to sue over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UnitedHealth Group is joining the ranks of insurers that are suing the feds over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings calculations.

Much like other recent lawsuits, the healthcare giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inappropriately used multiple measures in the calculations. Over the summer, a Georgia federal court sided with MA plan Clover Health, and tossed 20 measures that were used in its 2026 scores.

That legal ruling has been the basis of much of the current round of legal wrangling.

UnitedHealth said in its complaint that it is bringing the lawsuit to ensure "that their 2027 Star Ratings are calculated in accordance with CMS’s statutory authority and procedural obligations."

The star ratings are tied to quality bonus payments for Medicare Advantage plans and listed on the Medicare plan finder to help individuals identify high-quality coverage. When those payments are lower due to a decline in scores, the insurer may not be as nimble in lowering premiums or enhancing benefits.

"The Star Ratings carry real consequences," UnitedHealth wrote in the complaint. "A plan’s Star Rating thus directly affects the benefits and healthcare offerings that Medicare beneficiaries receive."

Elevance Health is the latest insurer to sue the feds over its performance in the latest round of star ratings for the Medicare Advantage program.

The company sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in District of Columbia federal court on Friday, arguing that the 2027 star ratings calculations violated the Administrative Procedure Act in using 11 measures that it says were adopted unlawfully.

In the lawsuit, the company said that the harm from including these measures is "concrete and substantial." If they were excluded, it would increase the scores for 12 of its Medicare Advantage contracts and generate $516 million in additional quality bonus payments.

"Their inclusion therefore does more than violate statutory requirements in the abstract: it depresses Elevance Health’s ratings and reduces the funding available for the following payment year," per the lawsuit. "That funding could support broader supplemental benefits, lower premiums and cost-sharing, and improved care coordination."

"CMS’s unlawful methodology puts those resources out of reach," the company said.

In addition to the financial impacts, Elevance argues that the star ratings scores can also lead to reputational damage that makes it harder for them to compete in the MA market. It also provides prospective enrollees with inaccurate information, the company said.

"Beneficiaries cannot make informed coverage choices when the government’s own comparison tool conveys a distorted assessment of the plans available to them," Elevance said.

"An artificially depressed rating does not merely place Elevance Health at a competitive disadvantage; it undermines the very comparison the program is supposed to enable," the company continued. "A rating lowered by unlawful measures presents beneficiaries with a misleading signal of relative quality, rather than a lawful basis for distinguishing among competing plans."

CVS Heath's Aetna is joining the ranks of insurers suing over its results in the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

The insured filed suit Monday in Georgia's Southern District Court, and argues that 28 measures used by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to calculate its scores were "unlawfully adopted" and should have been excluded.

The court is the same venue that ruled in favor of Clover Health over the summer, and set aside 20 measures that were used to determine its 2026 scores. That decision, which the feds have appealed, kicked off a broad recalculation of 2026 scores that looked different for insurers outside of Clover, triggering a wave of litigation.

In its lawsuit, Aetna cites the Clover decision in finding that CMS extended beyond its statutory authority in deploying those 20 measures.

The company said that calculating its scores using the 28 measures in question will likely cost it $2 billion in 2028 quality bonus payments and rebate retention. Those are funds that the insurer could "apply toward expanding member benefits, reducing premiums and investing in quality improvement."

Aetna adds that in addition to the monetary loss, having lower scores negatively impacts the company's reputation and its ability to attract potential members.

"The harm to CVS Health is not exclusively financial; lower ratings carry meaningful reputational harm, which can in turn impact membership," per the lawsuit. "By incorporating unlawful measures into the 2027 Star Ratings calculation, CMS cast CVS Health’s ratings in a poorer light in the eyes of Medicare Advantage consumers relative to peer MAOs, undermining CVS Health’s ability to compete for Medicare beneficiaries through enhanced benefits and the like."

Aetna did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Based on an analysis from Stephens, 69% of Aetna's MA members are in plans with four or more stars for 2027, down from 81%. That threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments.

Aetna's complaint follows others focused on the 2027 scores from Centene and Alignment Healthcare (see those stories below).

Centene has become the latest insurer to sue the federal government over its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

In a lawsuit filed Thursday in Georgia's Southern District Court, the company argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services violated the Administrative Procedure Act in determining its latest scores. Centene says that CMS ran afoul of "core statutory safeguards" in deploying 17 measures.

The use of those measures ultimately caused "significant injury" to the company, according to the complaint. For 2027, 9% of Centene's members are enrolled in plans with at least four stars, which declined from 18% in the prior year.

"In implementing each of the individual Star measures that Centene challenges, CMS violated applicable law and thereby caused Centene to lose out on hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue that Centene could use to strengthen benefits, reduce premiums, and improve health outcomes," the company said in the lawsuit.

CMS argues that the court has already sided with a similar argument in its decision in favor of Clover Health earlier this year. In that case, which led to a broad recalculation in scores, the courts set aside 20 measures that were used in determining Clover's star ratings for 2026.

If the 17 measures in question had been excluded in calculating Centene's scores, the company estimates it would receive $448 million more in quality bonus payments for the 2028 plan year, funds it would deploy to expand benefits, lower premiums and enhance programs like care coordination.

In addition to the financial impact, a drop in star ratings also carries a reputational hit, Centene said.

"Beyond the financial impact to the company and its members, depressed ratings also inflict significant reputational damage and diminished membership," the company said in the complaint

Centene had not returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Alignment Healthcare sued federal regulators, alleging that its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings were determined "in flagrant violation" of statute.

In the lawsuit filed Friday in District of Columbia federal court, the insurer says that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services "has completely departed from Congress’s vision of leveraging predictable, valid measures developed with input from providers, plans, and the public" in establishing the methodology for the star ratings.

The company argues that rather than establish "consistent, stable specifications" for metrics through the traditional rule-making process, the agency instead detailed key measures through a series of "technical notes." This violates the Administrative Procedure Act, per the lawsuit.

The program's star ratings are the critical determinant in quality bonus payments to insurers as well as a tool that aims to make it easier for enrollees and brokers to identify benefits with the highest quality.

"Consistent application of the statutory requirements governing Star Ratings is therefore essential not only to plan payments and competition but also to ensuring that beneficiaries can rely on the Star Ratings as meaningful and comparable measures of plan quality," Alignment said in the lawsuit.

The company adds that multiple recent court decisions have set aside CMS' star ratings methodology, notably a ruling over the summer in favor of Clover Health that tossed 20 metrics used in the 2026 calculations. A Georgia federal judge determined that 10 measures utilized exceeded CMS' authority, while 10 other measures were promulgated inappropriately.

CMS recalculated the scores across the board following the ruling, but only set aside the 10 measures that the courts determined were outside the bounds of its regulatory authority. The agency maintained that approach in the 2027 calculations, Alignment argues.

"Congress created the Star Ratings program to allow Medicare Advantage beneficiaries to make informed decisions about plan enrollment based on clinically validated measures of plan quality that had been subjected to notice and comment," the company said. "CMS’s contrary approach fails to carry out the vision that Congress set forth by statute."

The Trump administration has appealed the Clover decision, so that legal case remains ongoing.

In addition, Alignment argues it suffered reputational and financial damage as a result of its 2027 scores, which plummeted compared to the prior year. Just 25% of its members are in plans with four or more stars for 2027, down from 100% in 2026.

Shares in the company tumbled following the release of the ratings, though stock prices have rebounded since.

Alignment sued the feds following the Clover decision to secure a recalculation for its scores that aligns with the court's decision, and in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, said that the lawsuit aligns with that perspective.

"Our lawsuit seeks to ensure that the Star Ratings program operates as Congress intended and that Alignment is properly compensated for the care we provide," Alignment said in the statement. "We respect the judicial process and will present our case in court. Because this matter involves pending litigation, we will not comment on the specific legal arguments beyond our filings."

"Our focus remains on delivering exceptional care, improving health outcomes and advocating for a stable, lawful regulatory framework that supports seniors and strengthens the Medicare Advantage program," the company said.

#5635. 5 Exciting Ways to Invest in Real Estate

When it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

With digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech company could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

#5634. Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

Crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen. In experiments involving two carrion crows, the birds needed an average of just 235 milliseconds to determine which way a pattern of moving dots was traveling and respond with their choice. Despite their remarkable speed, they remained highly accurate.

The findings, published in the journal Science, offer new insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions. Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen's Institute of Neurobiology found that the crows' rapid responses were accompanied by equally impressive activity in their brain cells.

Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy

To test the birds' decision-making abilities, the researchers presented them with moving dots on a touchscreen. The crows had to determine whether most of the dots were traveling left or right, then indicate their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen.

The birds performed remarkably well, even when the direction of movement was difficult to identify. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Philipp Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent."

The results showed that crows could evaluate visual information and make accurate choices in a fraction of a second. To understand how their brains accomplished this, the researchers examined the activity of individual neurons as the birds completed the task.

Crow Brains Begin Processing Decisions in Just 70 Milliseconds

The team recorded neural activity in a part of the bird brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This region plays an important role in processing information and making decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

The recordings revealed that the crows' brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions almost immediately. Just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared, neurons associated with the different choices were already showing distinct patterns of activity.

These signals emerged well before the birds physically responded. As the crows evaluated the moving dots, neural activity steadily increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. The activity reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the bird ultimately selected.

Different Brain Structures, Similar Decision-Making Processes

One of the most intriguing findings is that crows appear to make decisions using neural processes similar to those found in humans and other primates, even though their brains are organized very differently.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates," says Andreas Nieder.

Unlike mammals, birds do not have a cerebral cortex organized into layers. Nevertheless, their brains appear capable of following the same fundamental principles for evaluating evidence and reaching decisions. In this visual task, the crows completed that process twice as quickly as primates.

The researchers suggest that this exceptional speed could reflect the demands birds have faced throughout their evolution. Rapidly interpreting visual information and responding with precise movements are especially important for animals that fly and use their beaks to interact with their surroundings.

"Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging," Nieder explains.

However, the exact biological mechanisms responsible for the crows' speed advantage remain unknown. Further studies will be needed to determine how their differently structured brains can make comparable visual decisions so much faster than those of humans and monkeys.

#5633. FDA’s search for a new leader, and China’s largest drugmakers

By Adam Feuerstein, Elaine Chen, and Damian Garde

Adam Feuerstein is a senior writer and biotech columnist, reporting on the crossroads of drug development, business, Wall Street, and biotechnology. #5632. Agentic AI pushes the neocloud race beyond GPU counts toward global platforms

The neocloud boom is entering a sorting phase, and global cloud availability is emerging as the line between providers built for enterprise AI and those built to rent out racks of graphics processing units.

With agentic AI moving from pilots into production, buyers are looking past raw GPU counts toward integrated platforms they can build on. That shift is redrawing the competitive map for cloud AI infrastructure. Enterprise practitioners are now starting ambitious agentic AI agendas, and they need the full stack of services behind AI-native applications rather than standalone clusters, according to Kevin Cochrane (pictured, right), chief marketing officer of Vultr.

“There are those providers that are trusted platforms, that are global cloud platforms that have the totality of services that are required for real agentic AI deployments,” Cochrane said. “We’ll continue to see a separation of the pack and there’ll be those that are trusted platforms that enterprises can rely on and there’ll be those that aren’t.”

Cochrane and Duncan Ng (left), vice president of solutions engineering at Vultr, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why agentic AI is reviving demand for central processing units, how Vultr builds data centers as integrated systems and which neocloud providers are likely to survive consolidation. (* Disclosure below.)

Calling a service an enterprise cloud takes more than racking accelerators. Vultr organizes its footprint into data center regions, each of which can control multiple facilities on one network. Developers get one application programming interface they can hook into a Terraform template, Cochrane explained. Many rivals, by contrast, stood up individual sites quickly to serve bespoke customer contracts.

“In traditional neoclouds, the data centers are actually islands. They’re not connected. It’s not one unified global network. It’s not one unified global platform,” Cochrane said. “These are like individual data centers stood up very quickly for bespoke customer contract. That is not a platform.”

Agentic AI is also reshaping the hardware mix inside those regions. Reasoning models now let agents chain dozens of steps, call tools and validate results in flight — work that leans heavily on CPUs, according to Ng. Vultr ran a cloud for more than a decade before the GPU rush and has used processors from Advanced Micro Devices Inc. as the backbone of its CPU fleet for several years, he added. The company has since extended that partnership to accelerators with a $1.2 billion order for AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems.

“This increased density, this increased usage — these are just new hosting companies,” Ng said. “This is just a new application that is 10 times more compute dense than the last that we’re trying to sell to.”

Enterprises are finally moving those workloads out of pilot and into production, Ng noted. One Big Four global systems integrator uses Vultr as the substrate for a risk management service. Vultr has been rolling out platform upgrades aimed at enterprise agentic AI to support that kind of deployment.

“What they’re doing is something that used to take consulting hours, people poring through spreadsheets and poring through invoices, poring through declarations,” he said. “They now are able to automate significant portions of this to serve a larger number of their customers and do a deeper dive into their risk supply chains.”

#5631. CMS issues Medicare Advantage proposals aimed at boosting competition

CMS issues Medicare Advantage proposals aimed at boosting competition" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has proposed a slew of changes to Medicare Advantage and Part D designed to "revitalize care" in these markets.

For one, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said late Friday that it will update application and network adequacy requirements to make it easier for new entrants. The agency proposed to require organizations to demonstrate network adequacy during their first year in operation, rather than during the application process.

This shift would eliminate a significant barrier for new entrants, driving greater competition in the market.

CMS has also proposed combining three specialty areas in behavioral health — clinical psychology, clinical social work and outpatient behavioral health — into one specialty group for the purposes of network adequacy. The changes will give plans greater flexibility in building out behavioral health networks.

CMS will also make adjustments that seek to boost competition for special needs plans.

In addition, the agency said it will make adjustments to the star ratings program, focusing its ratings on 15 measures. The proposed measure set would emphasize "clinical outcomes and patient experience while retaining select process measures in high-priority areas where performance remains low."

CMS is also aiming to update the calculation methodology that will "raise the bar for achieving high ratings," and thus quality bonus payments.

"People with Medicare should be able to choose coverage based on what matters most to them — quality, affordability, and access," said CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These proposals are about creating a Medicare Advantage marketplace that rewards better care and better value while empowering beneficiaries with the options and knowledge they need to make informed decisions about their health."

The proposed rule also includes provisions that align with Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again agenda by setting a "healthy food" standard that MA plans should follow for supplemental benefits.

The goal, CMS said, is to ensure that Medicare dollars are spent on food benefits that align with MAHA.

"Medicare food benefits should pay for nutritious food that helps people improve their health and manage chronic disease," Kennedy said in the announcement. "This proposal would require those benefits to meet the Dietary Guidelines for Americans while preserving access to foods and nutritional products that providers recommend for patients’ specific medical needs."

"Under President Trump, we are putting prevention at the center of health care and demanding more from every Medicare dollar," Kennedy said.

#5630. Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy

A major study involving more than 750,000 pregnancies has uncovered an important difference in the potential pregnancy risks of popular weight loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. Women who unintentionally used these drugs shortly before or during early pregnancy were more likely to give birth prematurely, but only when the medications had been prescribed to treat existing diabetes.

Among women taking the same medications for weight management, researchers found no significant association with premature birth or other pregnancy complications examined in the study.

The findings suggest that diabetes itself, rather than the medications, may be responsible for the increased risk of early delivery. The research was published in Human Reproduction Open, a leading journal in reproductive medicine.

The medications examined included semaglutide (brand names: Ozempic, Wegovy) and liraglutide (Saxenda). Both belong to a widely used group of drugs known as GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs). Originally developed to manage type 2 diabetes, these medications also suppress appetite, making them effective treatments for weight loss. However, their safety during pregnancy has not been established.

Why Ozempic and Similar Drugs Raise Pregnancy Concerns

Professor Henriette Svarre Nielsen, who led the research at the Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics at Copenhagen University Hospital Hvidovre in Hvidovre, Denmark, explained that the rapid rise in GLP-1 prescriptions has created an urgent need for better information about pregnancy exposure.

"GLP-1 RA treatment has, within the last few years, become the medication with the sharpest increase in prescriptions worldwide. Current guidance suggests the treatment should be stopped eight weeks prior to planning a pregnancy. However, this is based on early-phase model organism studies, and not real-world evidence. Nonetheless, because of its widespread adoption, inadvertent exposure in early pregnancy is inevitable, and there is hardly any evidence to guide clinical counseling when it happens."

To investigate these concerns, researchers examined whether accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications around conception was associated with complications during pregnancy. They focused on preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks), pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, delivering a baby that was unusually large for its gestational age, stillbirth, and placental problems.

Study Examines More Than 750,000 Pregnancies

The research team used Denmark's nationwide health registries to examine 756,636 pregnancies involving a single baby among 480,231 women. All pregnancies resulted in deliveries between October 1, 2009, and December 31, 2023.

The researchers classified a pregnancy as having possible accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications if the woman filled a prescription for semaglutide or liraglutide during the eight weeks before or after the first day of her last menstrual period.

This 16-week period included the time when a woman might not yet realize she was pregnant, as well as the early stages of fetal development when major organs begin to form.

Of the pregnancies included in the study, 529 involved prescription records indicating exposure to GLP-1 medications during this period.

To make the comparisons more reliable, the researchers accounted for several characteristics that could influence pregnancy outcomes. These included maternal age, body mass index (BMI), smoking habits, location, education, and whether the woman already had diabetes. They also considered the month and year of pregnancy to account for possible seasonal patterns and changes over time.

Diabetes May Be the Key to Premature Birth Risk

The results revealed a striking distinction between women prescribed GLP-1 drugs for diabetes and those using them for weight loss.

Dr. Kathrine Hviid, the study's first author and a PhD student in the same department, said the findings could help shape future research and improve medical guidance for women who unknowingly use these drugs during early pregnancy.

"We made some extremely important findings that have implications for future studies, such as randomized controlled trials of GLP-1 RA usage in pregnancy, and for clinical counseling.

"We found that these medications were associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, but the risk was only present when the medication was used for diabetes treatment, and not for weight management. This suggests that the underlying condition of diabetes, rather than the medication, may be driving this association."

At first, women with GLP-1 prescriptions appeared to experience several pregnancy complications more frequently than those without exposure. However, most of these associations were no longer statistically significant once the researchers accounted for other factors that could affect pregnancy outcomes.

The remaining significant association involved premature birth among women who had been prescribed liraglutide or semaglutide to manage diabetes.

Compared with women who had not been exposed to these medications, the adjusted odds of premature delivery were 70% higher among women taking liraglutide for diabetes and 84% higher among those taking semaglutide for diabetes.

The researchers' accompanying announcement also reported estimated increases of approximately 11% for semaglutide and 9% for liraglutide among women with pre-existing diabetes.

Crucially, the same elevated risk of premature birth was not observed when the medications were prescribed specifically for weight management.

This difference suggests that the underlying medical condition may play a larger role in pregnancy outcomes than exposure to the medications themselves.

What the Findings Mean for Women Taking GLP-1 Drugs

According to Professor Nielsen, future investigations must distinguish between women taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes and those using them for weight control. Combining these groups could obscure important differences in their underlying health and pregnancy risks.

"Future studies must take account of the reason a woman has been prescribed these medications, as the risks differ between women using GLP-1 RAs for diabetes versus weight management. This is one of the first studies to examine GLP-1 RA exposure in early pregnancy according to the reason for prescription. As more evidence accumulates, these findings will guide clinical counseling for women inadvertently exposed to GLP-1 RAs in early pregnancy. In Denmark, about 70% of people who use weight loss medications are women and so it is inevitable that some may take it without realizing they are pregnant."

Although the results provide useful new information, Nielsen emphasized that additional research is necessary before changing existing medical recommendations.

In particular, the findings do not justify abandoning current guidance to discontinue GLP-1 medications before a planned pregnancy. They also do not provide enough evidence to establish new clinical counseling recommendations based on why the drugs were prescribed.

Important Limitations of the Pregnancy Study

One of the investigation's greatest strengths was its size, with health records covering more than three-quarters of a million pregnancies.

However, the study was observational, meaning it could identify associations but could not determine whether GLP-1 medications directly caused premature births. Other factors, including the effects of diabetes itself, may help explain the results.

Another limitation was that the researchers relied on prescription records. Although they could determine whether a woman had filled a prescription, they could not confirm whether she had actually taken the medication.

The researchers nevertheless believe that most women who purchased the drugs were likely to have used them because of their substantial cost.

In Denmark, patients generally contribute toward the cost of GLP-1 injections, although government subsidies are available for diabetes treatment. For example, a 1mg injection of Wegovy or Ozempic (semaglutide) costs approximately €180 and €114, respectively, with the diabetes subsidy reflected in the lower price.

Dr. Hviid said: "Because of the high cost, we assume that compliance is very high among the women prescribed GLP-1 RAs."

Experts Call for More Individualized Pregnancy Guidance

The findings also attracted attention from researchers outside Denmark.

In an invited commentary published alongside the study, Drs. Yeyi Zhu and Monique Hedderson of Kaiser Permanente Northern California and the Center for Upstream Prevention of Adiposity and Diabetes Mellitus in Pleasanton, California, described the results as important additions to the growing research on GLP-1 medications and reproductive health.

They wrote that the findings "complement and extend an emerging evidence base on the reproductive safety of GLP-1 RAs."

The researchers also emphasized that the distinction between diabetes treatment and weight management could help doctors provide more personalized advice to women who accidentally used these medications around conception.

"For clinicians, the study by Hviid et al. (2026) may inform preconception and early pregnancy counseling. The observation that elevated preterm birth risk was confined to women treated for diabetes, and not to those using GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight management, supports more balanced, individualized discussions with patients who may have experienced inadvertent periconceptional exposure. For patients with diabetes, the study reinforces the importance of recognizing diabetes as an important risk factor for obstetric complications and prioritizing metabolic health and glycemic management before and during pregnancy."

Ultimately, the study highlights why a woman's underlying health conditions matter when evaluating the potential pregnancy risks of GLP-1 medications. While the findings offer some reassurance regarding accidental exposure among women using these drugs for weight loss, they do not establish that the medications are safe during pregnancy.

Further research will be needed to clarify the risks and determine how best to counsel women who become pregnant while using these increasingly popular treatments.

#5629. Patients have little say in how brain implant trials are done. Ian Burkhart wants to change that

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Disability in Health Care Reporting Fellow

Rose covers disability and mental health, and she helps write STAT’s daily Morning Rounds newsletter. Confidential tips can be sent to Rose on Signal at rosebroderick.11.

So you’ve been diagnosed with ALS — what now? Maybe you join a clinical trial for a brain implant that could help you do things like move your hand or talk to your loved ones. But can you influence the research as a participant? And what happens to the data collected from your brain when the study ends?

A new report addresses these and other questions, exploring how trials of implanted brain-computer interfaces can better address the interests and concerns of participants, who often join in a last-ditch attempt to improve their communication, mobility, or autonomy.

“These studies can sometimes last years, and it becomes a big part of someone’s life. You want there to be as much agency from the participant as possible,” said Ian Burkhart, who co-founded the coalition, with other participants in early studies of implantable BCI devices, to share patient feedback with developers and researchers. Burkhart said the report emerged out of discussions between him and other study participants, who felt they had very little say in how trials were conducted.

The recommendations arrive as the field moves from a niche, proof-of-concept phase into a humming neurotechnology startup ecosystem with eager investors and multiple clinical trials testing implanted devices’ safety and efficacy. Ethicist Anna Wexler believes that scientists need better policies to ensure participants’ rights and autonomy.

“There is no good solution right now. We talk about potentially mandatory insurance policies, escrows, and institutions committing support, but right now we just don’t actually have solutions,” Wexler, a University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine professor, said during a panel at a recent brain-computer interface industry conference in New York.

STAT spoke with Burkhart about his own experiences as someone with tetraplegia and as a former BCI user shopping around for his next device. He wants to make sure that during his next trial, he has more clarity around the study’s overall expectations, what he can do with the data generated, and what will happen to his care after he is explanted.

You were implanted in 2014 with a device at Ohio State University that helped you move your arm. What happened when the study ended?

When our study was starting to wind down because of some funding issues, the institutional review board said, “Well, we can just have them have the device taken out, and then if it gets funded again, they can just put another one back in.” Like, that’s great when it’s not you that’s going through experimental brain surgery.

To me, it really just minimized my experience down to something more akin to a lab rat versus being a human. The [IRB and the institution] claim to be supportive of the researchers trying to get additional funding and continue the work. And if they really were, they would have seen that it makes more sense to put a little bit more of a pause on it and wait for funding to come through if possible, instead of doing something as disruptive as having surgery.

Most informed consents right now, they’re more of a one-sided agreement protecting the research team and institution versus protecting what the participants may want. If you don’t agree to something, the alternative is to not participate. And that’s fine when you’re first signing up for a study. It changes once you’ve already been in a study and you’re re-consenting to continue on with the study, especially when there are very limited alternatives for treatment for this patient population.

Yes. And then, you know, you add in the psychological piece of using these devices to restore function after a disability. To my knowledge, everyone that’s used a device has an acquired disability versus being born with their disability. So they have that capability, and then they have their disability, and that capability is taken away from them, and then these devices help restore some of that function, and then it’s taken away again.

If there’s real technical reasons that the device stops working or we’re not able to use this technology anymore, that’s one thing. But if there’s just a well, it’s easier for us to administratively close the study, and we can start it back up again in the future, that doesn’t seem like a valid reason to take away and have someone psychologically experience a little bit of their injury or their disability again.

How does that compare to other BCI users’ experiences?

They have had similar experiences where they don’t really know what the end of the study is going to look like. And as a participant, you can leave at any time, but also the researchers can kick you out of the study at any time, within their rationale.

It’s a little bit of a challenge there when you are doing something as intimate as going into the lab multiple times a week, multiple hours at a time, and it becomes such a big part of your life. For it to just be abruptly stopped can be really challenging. … You know, Nathan Copeland, he’s passed 11 years [with a device] now.

That’s practically a millenium in this fledgling industry. What should long-term care look like for BCI users?

We’re past the proof of concept phase [for these devices]. Is there any support for people to maintain these devices, not in a way that you know we’re forcing a company or institution to keep up a manufacturing line, but can there be decisions made earlier on that will allow, if you need a new battery, you can get a battery from company A, B, or C? Versus it’s only one company that makes the battery, and if that company’s out of business, then you’re done? What kind of support can be available so that you can potentially slowly wind down the trial and not have it be as abrupt?

I knew when I signed up [for my study] that this wasn’t going to be a forever thing. It was only supposed to be up to a year and a half, but it continued, we were able to reconsent and expand on the study, and it became a much larger part of my life than I envisioned. To then have such an abrupt ending is not something that anyone wants to go through.

I only had access to the device when I’m going to the lab. Now that people are using these devices at home and you know out in the wild, it’s a much more significant change when there is that abrupt end.

The report talks a lot about giving participants more access to their neural data. What are you proposing?

If you give the participant full ownership of that data, there should be a mechanism where the main research team can have first crack at that data, but then after, if the participant agrees, it allows them to open that up and let other researchers who may not have the resources to implant an individual and capture all this data to see what they can learn from that as well.

I feel like I would balk at that if I was a researcher or regulator.

It really just depends on what information it is, how much of a kind of delay that someone may get, and how exactly those experiments are structured. If I could have shared some of the raw data from my study, so someone sitting around in their basement trying to come up with different decoding algorithms, I think that’s beneficial for the field. And you know, if the researchers are actually motivated by what’s beneficial for the field versus getting their credit and publishing another paper and moving on, I think they would be open to that.That’s really the goal out of these types of devices to help individuals with disabilities have more independence, autonomy, agency over their lives.

Are a lot of study participants asking to run raw data through decoding algorithms in their basement?

I’ve certainly met a few. Most of the participants were like, “That’s way over my head.” But I think that there are plenty of people who would like to put their neural data into an AI tool and see what they can learn.

My study has been over for six years now. All that data is hopefully still sitting on a server somewhere. I’m sure there’s something that someone with a fresh set of eyes could make sense of, potentially bringing a little bit of value.

I certainly think it would be interesting to see what I can find out about my own data, being able to go into the research lab but then, on my own time, I can sit at home and run some other experiments that might be different. Get as much juice out of it as we can. Make sure it’s worth the squeeze.

#5628. Researchers explore possibility of a CTE blood test

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Jason is a general assignment reporter, with particular focus on genetic medicine and rare disease. Confidential tips can be sent on Signal at JasonMast.77.

Rose covers disability and mental health, and she helps write STAT’s daily Morning Rounds newsletter. Confidential tips can be sent to Rose on Signal at rosebroderick.11.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.

Good morning, everyone. Are you a fan of “Grand Theft Auto”? Will your boss not give you the day off to play the video game you’ve been waiting 13 years for? Don’t worry, DJ Khaled and Dr. Xbox have you covered. Just click here and fill out the form. You’ll have a diagnosis and doctor’s note for Vitamin G deficiency faster than a telehealth company can prescribe you a peptide.

Unapproved and off-label peptide drugs have long been popular with bodybuilders looking for an edge, but they could soon become a mass market health product, thanks to new initiatives from two popular telehealth companies.

Hims & Hers unveiled Thursday its Peptides+ program, offering two peptides alongside several compounded medications popular among peptide users. Noom announced its own offerings this week as well. This follows a decision by FDA leaders to — despite the concerns of staff scientists – allow compounders to produce six peptides that haven’t been approved by the agency, including BPC-157 and TB-500. Hims said it will soon offer BPC-157 and TB-500; Noom is considering adding them too.

Telehealth companies argue their peptides will be safer and more reliable than the black market “research-grade” products often used today, and Hims notes its program will offer twice-yearly blood tests for patient monitoring. But critics contend selling drugs that haven’t gone through the FDA’s approval process for their proposed use will bring products that have not been proven safe or effective to many patients who would not have otherwise encountered them.

A few of the largest U.S. drugmakers recently told a Congressional committee they would not start new clinical trials in the Xinjiang region of China or in hospitals affiliated with the Chinese military.

The concessions come as U.S. pharmas rush to partner with Chinese biotech startups and hospitals, alarming some American lawmakers. Last year, the House Select Committee on China opened investigations into Merck, Eli Lilly, AbbVie, Pfizer, and Bristol Myers Squibb over concerns about intellectual property exposure, military entanglements, and ethical standards at trial sites. All five of those companies have now agreed to not start any new trials at hospitals with ties to the People’s Liberation Army.

Four — all but AbbVie — agreed to stop trials in Xinjiang, where the Chinese government has targeted Uyghurs and other ethnic and religious minorities. AbbVie cited a “duty to provide potentially lifesaving treatment to patients there, most of whom company officials stated are oncology patients in a critical state of disease,” according to the committee, which is releasing a report today about its findings.

That’s how long journals should generally take to review potentially problematic studies, according to a report from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine.

The 157-page document comes after a raft of papers from high-profile scientists at places like Stanford University and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute were alleged to contain doctored data, contributing to distrust in scientific institutions. The authors found that allegations don’t always lead to retractions, even when they should. They encouraged journals to be more aggressive in retracting studies, and urged editors to review concerns raised within four weeks. Researchers, in turn, should not argue a study should remain up because errors in one section don’t impact the overall findings.

The National Academies’ report was supposed to be released publicly Thursday morning. But as of Thursday evening, it had not been published on the nonprofit’s website, though advanced copies were sent to media outlets. Jennifer Walsh, a National Academies spokesperson, told STAT in an email that “the report is being paused pending further review of some of the citations.” She did not provide a new release time. Reporting by Science alleges that 10 of the report’s references contain apparently fabricated first names for co-authors, suggesting that a large language model may have written the references.

Neurologists trying to treat or prevent CTE, the degenerative brain disease caused by repeated blows to the head, have long been hampered by the fact that the disease can only be diagnosed after death, with an autopsy. But on Thursday, researchers published data that could one day lead to a CTE blood test.

The key was 21 football players who donated blood while they were alive and then gave their brains to the Boston University CTE Center Brain Bank after death. Eighteen had confirmed CTE, by autopsy; among those 16 had advanced disease. Researchers found a particular form of tau — the toxic protein tangles that build up in the brains of patients with CTE and other neurodegenerative disorders — was elevated in those 18 volunteers’ blood, relative to those who didn’t have CTE. And subjects with advanced CTE had higher blood levels of this form of tau, called eMTBR-tau, than those with mild CTE.

“While there is still much work to do to validate these findings before the test is ready to use in patients, I am very hopeful that this study marks a major milestone in our ability to diagnose and ultimately treat this devastating disease,” co-author Gil Rabinovici Edward at the University of California San Francisco said in a statement.

The National Institutes of Health may soon have an office dedicated to disability health research.

The Senate Appropriations Committee’s budget recommendations for the next fiscal year, released Wednesday, urge the NIH to establish a “centralized disability research office” and fulfill the agenda laid out in the agency’s strategic plan for this health disparity group.

If the office is created, it will have a tall task on its hands. More than a quarter of Americans have a disability, but many are routinely excluded from clinical trials. Take dementia and Alzheimer’s research. The federal government now spends $3.9 billion annually on dementia research, but clinical trials for Alzheimer’s therapeutics have excluded people with Down syndrome for decades, even though 90% of people with Down syndrome will develop Alzheimer’s by the age of 55.

The budget is not a one-to-one reflection of Congress’s budget next year, so there’s no guarantee that this office will be created. But advocates cheered the inclusion on social media. – O. Rose Broderick

#5627. The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in New York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.
