#5593. A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death

A daily nap may seem like a harmless way to recharge, but new research suggests that certain napping habits could provide important clues about a person's health as they age. Scientists have found that taking longer or more frequent naps, particularly in the morning, is associated with an increased risk of death among older adults.

Researchers from Mass General Brigham and Rush University Medical Center examined the napping patterns of 1,338 older adults over a period of up to 19 years. Their findings, published in JAMA Network Open, suggest that monitoring daytime sleep could help identify underlying medical conditions or early signs of declining health.

"Excessive napping later in life has been linked to neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases and even greater morbidity, but many of those findings rely on self-reported napping habits and leave out metrics like when and how regular those naps are," said lead author Chenlu Gao, PhD, an investigator in the Department of Anesthesiology at Mass General Brigham and an affiliated research fellow in the Division of Sleep and Circadian Disorders in the Department of Medicine. "Our study is one of the first to show an association between objectively measured nap patterns and mortality and suggests there is immense clinical value in tracking napping patterns to catch health conditions early."

Why Scientists Are Studying Daytime Napping

Daytime naps are common among older adults, with estimates suggesting that 20% to 60% regularly nap. An occasional nap can help restore energy and improve alertness, but excessive daytime sleeping in later life has been associated with several health concerns.

Despite these connections, researchers still have an incomplete understanding of how specific napping behaviors relate to long-term health. Many earlier studies depended on participants remembering and reporting their own sleep habits, which may not provide an accurate picture. They also often overlooked important details, such as how long naps lasted, when they occurred, and how much napping patterns changed from one day to the next.

To obtain more reliable measurements, the research team analyzed information from the Rush Memory and Aging Project. Launched in 1997, this long-running study was designed primarily to investigate memory, thinking abilities, and neurological decline among older adults in northern Illinois, most of whom were white.

Starting in 2005, participants wore wrist activity monitors for 10 days to record their daily periods of rest and movement. Researchers used these measurements to identify daytime sleep and assess nap duration, frequency, timing, and daily variation.

Longer and More Frequent Naps Linked to Higher Mortality Risk

By 2025, researchers had assembled up to 19 years of follow-up information from 1,338 participants. They then examined whether napping habits measured during the initial assessment were associated with the likelihood of dying from any cause during the subsequent years.

The results revealed several notable patterns. Older adults who slept longer during the day or took naps more frequently had higher mortality rates. The timing of naps also appeared to matter.

Each additional hour spent napping per day was associated with approximately a 13% higher mortality risk. Taking one additional nap per day was linked to about a 7% increase in risk.

One of the most striking findings involved morning naps. Participants who napped in the morning had a 30% higher mortality risk compared with those who napped in the afternoon.

However, not every aspect of napping was associated with poorer outcomes. Researchers found no increased mortality risk linked to irregular napping schedules, suggesting that changes in nap timing or duration from day to day were not necessarily indicators of greater risk.

Could Napping Habits Reveal Hidden Health Problems?

The researchers emphasize that their findings do not mean daytime naps directly cause health problems or shorten lives. Instead, excessive napping may reflect medical conditions or changes in the body that have not yet been recognized.

"It is important to note that this is correlation, not causation. Excessive napping is likely indicating underlying disease, chronic conditions, sleep disturbances, or circadian dysregulation," said Gao. "Now that we know there is a strong correlation between napping patterns and mortality rates, we can make the case to implement wearable daytime nap assessments to predict health conditions and prevent further decline."

These findings raise the possibility that wearable activity trackers could eventually become useful tools for monitoring health in older adults. By identifying changes in daytime sleep habits, healthcare professionals might be able to recognize warning signs of underlying illness, disrupted sleep cycles, or neurological decline earlier.

Although further research is needed to determine how effectively napping patterns can predict specific medical conditions, the study suggests that something as ordinary as a daily nap could provide valuable information about a person's overall health.

Study Authorship, Disclosures, and Funding

Authorship: In addition to Gao and Li, the Mass General Brigham researchers involved in the study include Ruixue Cai, Xi Zheng, Arlen Gaba, Lei Gao, and Kun Hu. Other contributors include Lei Yu, Aron S. Buchman, and David A. Bennett.

Disclosures: Li received a financial gift from iFutureLab to support research and has received consulting payments for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Cardiac Dynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Li also received an honorarium for delivering a lecture at Shandong University.

Hu has received consulting fees for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Medical Biodynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Mass General Brigham reviewed and managed the interests of both Li and Hu under its conflict of interest policies. These interests are unrelated to the present research.

Funding: The research received support from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine Foundation (290-FP-22), the Alzheimer's Association Research Fellowship to Promote Diversity (AARFD-22-928372), and the National Institute on Aging (RF1AG064312; R01AG083799).

Gao C. received additional funding from the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute (5T32HL007901). Li received support from the BrightFocus Foundation (A2020886S) and startup funding from the Department of Anesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital. Hu also received startup funding from the same department.

Gao L. received additional support from the Alzheimer's Association (AACSF-23-1148490), National Institute on Aging (R03AG087439), American Academy of Sleep Medicine (352-DS-24), and National Institute of General Medical Sciences (R35GM160254).

The Rush Memory and Aging Project was funded by the National Institutes of Health (R01AG056352 and R01AG017917).

#5592. What we learned from Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

Nvidia Corp. reported its quarterly results this week, and contrary to the prevailing narrative, the sky didn’t fall.

Revenue more than doubled year-over-year. The Vera Rubin chip platform achieved the fastest product ramp in the company’s history, and management raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to roughly 75%, up from 70%. By all accounts, it was a solid beat and raise.

This was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was announced on Nov. 12. Board Chair Harvey Jones told investors that the resignation followed the “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” Hours after Huang publicly said he would be willing to return, Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and would not take questions about the circumstances or the board’s ongoing investigation.

Colette Kress, the longtime chief financial officer who is now also serving as interim CEO, set the tone in her first minute: “Our ambition will not change. Our passion for innovation will not change, and our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change.”

After listening to the call, I believe Nvidia answered the short-term question and left the long-term one open. The company made a convincing case that it can execute without its founder. It has yet to show who decides where it goes next. Here are five things we learned and what they mean for those who buy, budget for or operate artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The fear going into the call was disruption. The quarter closed before Huang’s exit, so the results can’t settle that. The guidance can, and it went up. Hyperscalers brought Vera Rubin into production in about a month, half the time Grace Blackwell required. The roadmap is set through Vera Rubin Ultra next year and Feynman in 2028, and Kress said the supply agreements extend through the end of the decade.

She explained that the past month has been “Business as usual.” Kress added, “We’ve engaged with our customers, suppliers and partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” She also noted that TSMC leadership was at Nvidia’s offices this week.

I have long held that Nvidia’s moat was never the silicon. It’s the accumulated layers of systems, software and supply chain built around it. The past week was the first real test of that view, and so far, it’s holding. A yearly product cadence this complex runs on thousands of engineers and a supply chain planned years in advance.

Asked about talent retention, Kress acknowledged that “there are diverse opinions” among employees while insisting they are “committed to doing their life’s work” at Nvidia. The company’s talent can’t be overstated, and although Huang was the face of the company, the employees are what made it tick.

Earlier this week, Cisco Systems Inc. CEO Chuck Robbins appeared with Brian Sozzi. When asked whether he still trusts Nvidia, Robbins replied immediately, “Absolutely.” He added, “The industry’s bigger than one person. I don’t care how good you are. There are a lot of smart people. There are 42,000 people at Nvidia. So I’m not all that concerned.” Huang may have been the most visible Nvidia employee, but the company is full of smart, driven people. Leadership understands this, and I expect turnover to have minimal impact.

Employee retention is a top-of-mind issue for Nvidia executives. Business Insider reported this week that the company held its first all-hands meeting after Huang. The article noted that Kress announced plans to accelerate pay raises and equity grants, Jones discussed the CEO search and Buck outlined the roadmap. It’s reasonable to believe that Huang’s departure was a shock to employees, but the business goes on, and I expect things to settle down in short order.

For information technology buyers, nothing changes about what you’ve ordered or planned over the next 18 to 24 months. Don’t pause a deployment because of a leadership headline. The advice I gave in August still applies: Welcome Nvidia’s simplification and hedge the dependency.

One of the more interesting comments on the call came from Jones, not Kress. In describing the CEO search, which will consider both internal and external candidates, he said the board “appreciates that we’re living in a world where advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are driving major changes in our marketplace. Our new CEO will need to navigate those waters carefully.”

That was paired with immediate action. On the morning of earnings, the board created a standing national security and export control oversight committee of three directors that will retain outside experts. Kress disclosed that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China and noted that the U.S. Commerce Department issued new export controls this week, which the company “still has some time to study.”

Huang was a product visionary who also served as the industry’s chief diplomat. The board is now signaling that fluency in Washington is a core requirement, on par with technical vision.

For IT leaders at multinationals, export policy is now a deployment variable. The new Commerce rule is intended to block remote access to advanced chips via data centers in third countries, so the location of your capacity and who can access it are now compliance questions. Bring your compliance team into AI infrastructure planning early.

With demand still far ahead of supply, who gets Nvidia systems matters more than what they cost. Kress laid out the criteria more clearly than I’ve heard before. First are land, power and shell, meaning whether a customer’s facility is ready to receive and use the gear in the quarter it ships. Second is capital. Third, for customers that aren’t investment-grade, is proof of off-take, or evidence that someone has committed to use the capacity.

“All are getting the same pricing,” Kress said. “That is super important for us, and we just need to assure that they are ready on their side in terms of being able to accept the compute.”

Those same factors were incorporated into the guidance. Kress said the outlook “considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.” The reality is that the AI bottleneck has shifted from the chip to the building, the grid and the balance sheet. Nvidia is serving as the industry’s underwriter, determining who is ready.

The lesson for enterprise buyers is that readiness is the currency. If you want on-premises systems, secure power, cooling and funding before requesting allocation. If you can’t, buy capacity from a provider that has already cleared this hurdle. In my view, this also helps explain why sovereign AI is growing so quickly for Nvidia. Those projects often arrive with land and power already in place.

Over the past year, Nvidia has used its balance sheet to seed the ecosystem through guarantees, investments, and commitments to neoclouds and AI labs. Though  neoclouds remain important, Kress brought a different tone to this audience. She said Nvidia will “continue to be disciplined and selective” in supporting neoclouds and that it is “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees” as other sources of capital become available. Asked about vendor financing, she acknowledged that “a lot of things have changed over this last quarter.”

Two notable details emerged during the call. When Bernstein Research analyst Stacy Rasgon pressed on what he read as new disclosure language about neocloud commitments, Kress explained that Nvidia’s guarantees take effect only after a partner has raised its own debt and equity, built the facility and installed the compute. If the project stalls, the guarantee lapses.

“Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No,” she said. Even so, spelling it out clarifies Nvidia’s participation in neoclouds. When asked about uses of capital beyond the share buyback, which she said Nvidia still plans to complete, she put suppliers first: “The top priority is going to be our suppliers.” Prepayments to expand capacity come before customer financing, which will be reserved for “very strong customers.”

This was a critical piece of information for investors. I’ve previously compared vendor-financed neoclouds to the CLECs of the internet era, where the financing organization was left holding the bag. A CFO-led Nvidia appears to see the same risk. The result is a shakeout in which well-capitalized neoclouds with contracted demand grow stronger, while thinly funded ones struggle to secure systems. This should offer some comfort to investors that circular financing has been de-risked.

The flip side is that someone still must fund the buildout outside the hyperscalers. Kress pointed to infrastructure capital partners establishing financing platforms. Whether that money arrives as fast as Nvidia steps back is what to watch for.

My advice to IT buyers is to ask, before signing a multiyear deal with a neocloud, how it’s financed, how much capacity is committed and where it stands in Nvidia’s allocation queue. Those were niche questions a year ago. They should be standard due diligence now.

The demand story has shifted from training models to running agents, broadening what customers need from Nvidia. Citing OpenRouter data, Kress said agentic workloads now account for roughly 80% of tokens. Falling token prices are driving more usage, keeping GPU rental rates climbing.

The CPU growth story shouldn’t surprise anyone. In May, I wrote that agentic AI opens a massive new spigot for Nvidia on the CPU side. This quarter, demand outpaced supply. “Agentic AI is driving extraordinary demand for CPUs, far outstripping supply,” Kress said, noting that Nvidia’s Vera CPU is now adopted by CoreWeave, Meta, Nscale and Open AI. Agents spend much of their time calling tools, running code and moving data, which is general-purpose work. A CPU shortage amid a GPU boom shows how quickly the workload is changing.

Nvidia is also filling in the layers above and around the hardware. The agent safety platform pairs OpenShell, which limits what agents can access, with Sentry, which runs on BlueField data processing units and monitors agent behavior in silicon. In my view, the biggest barrier to deploying agents in production is control, not model quality.

The network is part of this, too. Kress said co-packaged optics is in volume production, and Lambda’s deployment, announced at this week’s SC26 conference, is the first large-scale proof point. Nvidia is a formidable networking vendor, though buyers mixing accelerators will still want to weigh a network supplier that isn’t also selling a competing chip.

For IT buyers, plan CPU capacity for agent workloads now, and insist that agent controls reside outside the model, in infrastructure you can audit.

The question of who the new CEO will be might not be just about Nvidia but about the entire industry. If the board goes internal, Ian Buck seems to be the frontrunner. Externally, the names most bandied about are Advanced Micro Devices Inc. CEO Lisa Su, Arm Ltd. CEO Rene Haas and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian, or we could see Manuvir Das make a comeback and return to the company.

Most industry watchers describe Nvidia as a chip company, a view that is about a decade out of date. Nvidia’s value comes from the full systems it has built around its silicon. Each is a stack tailored to an industry: hardware, libraries, frameworks, pretrained models, simulation and developer tools, all tuned to work together.

The next CEO must treat silicon as a key layer of an open, secure, agentic enterprise stack. Enterprises won’t buy GPUs. They’ll buy outcomes: agents that run safely on governed data across clouds, on-premises and at the edge. Whoever runs Nvidia next must sell that outcome, play well within an ecosystem Nvidia doesn’t fully control, and make security a core part of the platform. Here are three dark-horse candidates to consider:

Matt Garman. The Amazon Web Services Inc. CEO has led the world’s largest cloud through the shift to AI. He knows what it takes to turn infrastructure into consumable services at enormous scale. Garman also lives the open-stack approach: AWS offers model choice, runs its own Trainium chips alongside Nvidia’s, and sells to enterprises that want flexibility rather than lock-in. He would bring operational discipline and a deep feel for the customer. The question is whether Nvidia’s biggest customer-turned-competitor can credibly lead the supplier.

Jeetu Patel, Cisco Systems Inc.’s president and chief product officer, is the best storyteller in enterprise tech after Huang himself. He has spent the past few years rebuilding Cisco’s portfolio around secure AI infrastructure, integrating networking, security and observability into a single platform. That is exactly the “open, secure, agentic” stack Nvidia must deliver. Patel thinks in platforms, moves quickly,and has been personally using AI agents to shape his product views. He also has deep enterprise credibility, which Nvidia needs more than additional credibility with hyperscalers.

Charlie Giancarlo, CEO of Everpure (formerly Pure Storage), may be the most underrated name here. He built networking businesses at Cisco, spent time in private equity, and has repositioned Pure as a data management company. Storage revenue is growing thanks to hyperscaler wins. Giancarlo understands that agentic AI depends on data and that the data layer and the network are where enterprise AI succeeds or fails. He is a systems thinker who has led a platform transition before.

Two final points on the CEO hire: For some reason, there is a tremendous amount of industry chatter that Jensen Huang was the only person at Nvidia with key relationships with suppliers, partners, and other ecosystem providers. I know for a fact that is not true. Nvidia’s leadership, which includes Buck, Deb Shoquist (executive vice president of operations), Nico Caprez (vice president of global AI development), Gilad Shainer and Kevin Deierling (networking leadership), Kress and others, all have deep relationships with the ecosystem.

Also, I wouldn’t expect the board to make a snap decision about its next CEO. The roadmap is baked beyond Feynman, and the company can continue for a couple of years, if needed. This is an important hire; the board should take its time and ensure it’s the right person.

This call confirmed what many industry watchers, including me, have long believed: The moat was built in layers, and those layers held. Supply is constrained, the roadmap is set and customers are still asking for more than Nvidia can build.

Kress closed the call by saying, “We’ve got this.” On execution, I believe her. Kress is a steady hand right now, and the discipline she brings to capital allocation should make the AI buildout healthier. The bets that created Nvidia’s position, though, were placed years before the market arrived. Post-Jensen, Nvidia will continue to perform as it did; as Robbins put it, no one is bigger than the industry.

My advice to IT buyers is to stick with current plans and closely monitor the CEO search. Since Nvidia’s roadmap is baked through Feynman and beyond, it can ride momentum for the next two years or longer.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5591. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5590. MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

While we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful. Sleep provides an important opportunity to clear away these substances. As we rest, waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) move through the brain, helping remove waste and maintain healthy brain function.

Researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain. Those stronger electrical signals, in turn, produce larger waves of CSF.

The finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health. Scientists want to determine whether increasing this fluid movement could sharpen thinking, strengthen memory, or slow neurodegenerative diseases associated with the accumulation of damaging proteins, including amyloid beta.

"We found that we were able to increase the size of the CSF flow wave during sleep, which as far as we know, there hasn't been a method to do before. Now that we can enhance CSF flow during sleep in healthy adults, we're really excited to bring this technology to clinical populations to see what effects we can have," says Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis led the research as senior author. The findings were published in Science Translational Medicine, with Joshua Levitt serving as lead author. Levitt recently completed his PhD at Boston University and previously worked as a visiting graduate student in Lewis' laboratory.

Cerebrospinal fluid is a transparent liquid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord, providing protection against physical injury. It also supports brain function by transporting nutrients, including glucose, and carrying away waste released by brain cells as they consume energy.

In 2019, Lewis demonstrated that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) could be used to observe the movement of CSF into and out of the brain during sleep. Her team found that this movement closely follows slow electrical brain waves, which are especially prominent during deep sleep.

Building on that discovery, the researchers wanted to understand whether deliberately strengthening these electrical waves would also increase the movement of CSF. Earlier experiments had shown that sounds presented at precisely the right moment could enhance slow brain waves.

"You can make more of these electrical slow waves through an auditory stimulus, if it comes at just the right time. Similar to a child on a swing, if you push them when they're at the right moment in their movement, you can make that swing go farther," Lewis says. "The challenge is: How do you find just the right time?"

To test the idea, the team used extremely short bursts of pink noise, each lasting just 50 milliseconds. Pink noise contains the full range of frequencies that humans can hear, much like white noise. However, its lower frequencies are more prominent, while higher frequencies are quieter. The result is a softer, more balanced sound reminiscent of steady rainfall or a waterfall heard from a distance.

Timing was essential. The researchers needed to deliver each burst of sound when a sleeping participant's slow brain waves reached their peak. To identify those moments, they monitored electrical activity using EEG while simultaneously measuring CSF movement with fMRI.

Combining the two measurements created a technical obstacle. The powerful magnetic fields used in fMRI interfere with EEG recordings, making it difficult to detect the brain's electrical signals accurately and quickly enough to synchronize the sound.

The team addressed this problem by creating a method that removes interference from EEG signals in less than 100 milliseconds. They also designed an algorithm capable of predicting when the next slow wave peak would occur, compensating for the small delay introduced by processing the signals. Together, these advances made it possible to play each burst of pink noise at the intended moment.

Stronger Brain Cleaning Waves During Sleep

The researchers tested their approach in 14 healthy volunteers. They found that the carefully timed sounds increased the size of both the brain's slow electrical waves and the accompanying CSF waves. Importantly, the sounds were quiet enough that they did not wake the participants.

The brain scans also helped explain how the process works. Slow electrical waves were associated with blood vessels narrowing and widening, creating a pumping effect that pushes CSF out of the brain. These slow waves occur during non-REM sleep and become increasingly pronounced as sleep deepens.

By enhancing the electrical waves, the researchers were able to strengthen the fluid movement associated with the brain's natural waste removal process. However, the study did not directly establish whether the stronger CSF waves actually removed more waste or improved sleep quality.

Could Pink Noise Improve Sleep and Help Fight Alzheimer's?

The researchers now want to investigate whether increasing CSF flow leads to more refreshing, restorative sleep, particularly for people who struggle with insomnia. Another major goal is to determine whether the technique can improve the brain's ability to clear harmful substances.

This possibility is especially relevant to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, which are associated with the accumulation of abnormal proteins in the brain. If stronger CSF movement ultimately translates into more effective waste removal, the approach could offer a new way to address one of the biological processes involved in these conditions.

"Brain waste clearance is really important for Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia, which are caused, in part, by the buildup of molecules like amyloid and tau in the brain. If we can improve brain waste clearance, we may be able to help prevent the buildups of these plaques that lead to disease," Levitt says.

The technology could eventually become accessible outside research laboratories. Levitt has launched a company that aims to develop a home device, potentially in the form of a headband, that would deliver sound at the appropriate moments during sleep to increase CSF flow.

For now, the results demonstrate that a simple auditory stimulus, when precisely synchronized with brain activity, can alter the fluid waves associated with the brain's nighttime cleaning process. Whether those changes can translate into better sleep, stronger memory, or protection against neurodegenerative disease remains an important question for future studies.

The research received funding from a McKnight Scholar Award, a Sloan Fellowship, a Pew Biomedical Scholars Award, the Simons Foundation Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, the MIT EECS Transformative Research Fund, the National Institutes of Health, the Corundum Convergence Institute, and the Panasonic Well Fellowship for AI and Wellness.

Materials provided by Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Original written by Anne Trafton. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5589. The Ultimate Playbook To Buying a Home Without 20% Down Using Grants and Assistance Programs

Buying a home can be an intimidating process, with the biggest hurdle for many being coming up with enough funds for a down payment.

Many people believe they need to put down at least 20% if they want a home. But that's not necessarily true.

Most buyers have down payments ranging from 3.5% to 20% of the sale price of the home they're buying, and there are many down payment assistance programs that can help aspiring homeowners pivot from home browser to homebuyer.

These programs can help buyers snag a home by providing cash that can go toward a down payment. There are even loan programs for certain qualified buyers that don't require any down payments. The array of offerings from federal, local, and private sources can take the form of looser loan requirements, outright grants of money, or tax credits, all of which make homeownership more affordable.

First-time homebuyers, often with certain qualifications, are often beneficiaries of the assistance. Lower-income buyers, those who serve in the military or are veterans, and those who purchase fixer-uppers or homes in rural areas might also be eligible for the help.

The assistance ranges greatly, from a grant of several thousand dollars to, at the high end, a savings of five figures over the life of the loan.

Down payment assistance can take several forms and can even help buyers circumvent the PMI payment.

While 20% down has been something of a gold standard for homebuyers, it's also the minimum that generally lets them avoid private mortgage insurance, or PMI, which is assessed because lenders believe the loan carries risk. This in turn raises the homebuyer’s monthly expenses.

Here's an example: PMI is typically 0.5% to 1% of the loan amount per year. So if buyers put down less than 20% and their mortgage is $300,000, their PMI would be between $1,500 and $3,000 per year. That would add about $125 to $250 per month on top of their mortgage payment, a significant charge. (Homeowners can have PMI canceled when the equity in their home surpasses 20%.)

So, while a buyer can also choose loans that require a down payment of just a single digit, that PMI can stretch a budget paper-thin. That's where down payment assistance can help.

At least 2,000 such programs exist across the country. Some are federal, but most tend to be at state and local levels, which is important to know when searching for help. Private organizations, from lenders to nonprofits, also work with borrowers who need help.

These programs might offer grants, loans, tax credits, or a combination of a couple of these benefits. Funding can come from our government, nonprofits, and private enterprises. Let’s take a closer look:

Grants might be the most desirable form of down payment assistance. Typically, a grant is fully forgiven at closing and never has to be paid back. Yes, we’re talking about free money!

About 7% of down payment help comes in the form of grants, says Veronica Khandelwal, vice president of HFA Relations at Down Payment Resource, which provides consumers with guidance on this kind of assistance. But there is a catch.

“Grants require owner occupancy," she says of the requirement for buyers to live in these properties. That's to make sure these loans don't go to investors or vacation-home buyers. "Some programs allow grants to be applied to multifamily purchases of one to four units so long as one of the units is occupied by the borrower."

Forgivable loans are another option. These loans need to be repaid only if a repayment trigger event occurs, such as the home being sold before the end of the term, the home being no longer owner-occupied, the title being transferred, or the loan being defaulted on.

Deferred-payment loans are also available. These are paid back either at the end of the loan term or if a repayment trigger occurs. So, while it’s not a gift, it will help homebuyers get over that down payment hurdle and buy a house they might otherwise not have been able to afford.

Repayable loans are another leg up on homeownership. They require borrowers to make monthly payments, like a typical loan. But here's the good part: They do so at interest rates starting as low as 0%. That helps spread the down payment and closing costs over a number of years, making it much easier to enter the housing market.

Some agencies also offer a combination of these forms of assistance. That could mean that a portion of the help will be forgiven (or “written off” with no repayment needed), while some will need to be repaid. Tax credits are sometimes offered as well, further sweetening the deal.

Each down payment assistance program will have its own rules and guidelines, but the vast majority are offered only for a home that buyers will live in as a primary residence.

Here are some of the more popular national options folks might access to help them to pivot from home shopper to homebuyer.

FHA (Federal Housing Authority) loans were created by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development for first-time homeowners (HUD). These mortgages allow as little as 3.5% for the down payment, provided buyers have a credit score of 580 or higher, along with other qualifying factors. The federal government insures these loans, and for that reason, banks are more willing to loan money to homebuyers who have neither top-tier credit nor loads of cash to put down on the purchase.

FHA Section 203(k) loans require only 3% down, provided qualifying buyers will live in the property, typically one that needs work, while they fix it up. For buyers hoping for a DIY route into a dream home, this could be a win-win. The cost of improvements is included in the loan so buyers can finance both the home and up to $35,000 in repairs.

But buyers beware: The cost of materials and construction labor has spiked since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, and work is taking much longer to be completed than ever before.

VA (U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs) loans might be offered directly by the VA or backed by the department. Several factors are considered, such as service history, duty status, income, and credit rating. But those who qualify can purchase a home with zero down as long as the sales price isn’t higher than the home’s appraised value.

Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are federally funded loans that can help buyers skirt steep down payments. The Home Possible, HomeReady, and HomeOne loans typically offer a 3% down payment mortgage to qualifying, lower-income homebuyers.

Good Neighbor Next Door is another HUD-sponsored program. In this case, law enforcement officers, teachers, firefighters, and emergency medical technicians can enjoy a substantial incentive in the form of a discount of 50% from the list price of the home in a community that is being revitalized. The buyer must live in the house for three years as a primary residence.

Teacher Next Door Grant is a program similar to the one above but is designed to help educators own their own homes. Grants to the tune of up to $8,000 in certain areas are possible with additional down payment assistance available in some circumstances.

The USDA (U.S. Department of Agriculture) Rural Home Loan Program was created to assist people buying homes in rural locations. For qualifying, single-family properties, loans might be available with no money down. There are maximum income limits and other qualifications to be eligible for one of these mortgages.

There are plenty of other programs available as well. Different states and cities, as well as individual lenders and nonprofits, can help prospective homebuyers get the financing they need. Folks should put their location and "down payment assistance" into a search engine, and take a look at what's available. They might see everything from Habitat for Humanity to local religious organizations pop up. Also,visit Down Payment Resource.

One other path to explore is whether a buyer's job provides down payment assistance. A lot of employers may offer assistance in  the form of a $10,000 loan that is forgivable after five years.

Down payments hit a four-year low at the start of 2026. The median payment fell to $23,400 and 12.8% in Q1 2026, down 19% and 1.2 ppts year over year.

However, down payments remain well above pre-pandemic levels, as more buying is happening in the lower-down-payment South and Midwest, even as the Northeast stays deeply competitive.

The Northeast posted the highest median down payment at $57,600, reflecting higher home prices and more competition. The Northeast also sees the largest gap between what buyers are paying as a down payment today compared to pre-pandemic.

Compared to 2019, the Northeast has seen down payments climb 236.8%, significantly more than the next closest gap of 134.0% in the Midwest. These trends are consistent with the persistent upward pressure on home prices in these regions as scarce inventory is met with sustained buyer demand.

Get ready for some good news. There are a lot of misconceptions about who qualifies for down payment assistance.

“Many people think these programs are only available to low-income borrowers, first-time homebuyers, or for properties that have sales price limits,” says Down Payment Resource's Khandelwal. “But if you look, you’ll find specialized programs designed to assist specific groups, including first-generation homebuyers, minorities, Indigenous people, people of color, veterans, those with government jobs, disabilities, and more.”

Here’s something else to smile about: A first-time homebuyer doesn't just mean someone who's never bought a home before.

The federal government generally holds a broader definition of a first-time homebuyer. It’s someone who has not been a homeowner in the past three years. If you sold a house three-and-a-half years ago, you qualify as first-time buyer.

Buyers can take several different steps to find a down payment assistance program that’s right for them.

Check the federal programs mentioned above (like HUD, VA, USDA, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac), and see if there’s anything suitable.

Buyers should also visit their state’s Department of Housing website and see what might be listed, or call their number and inquire what down payment assistance programs might be available. Cities, towns, private lenders, and nonprofits may also have help.

“Homebuyers should seek the assistance of a mortgage lender who specializes in affordable lending to identify their best options,” advises Khandelwal.

In terms of what is typically needed to access aid, the documentation is very much in line with what’s needed to apply for any mortgage. Buyers will likely need the following:

Pay stubs plus W-2s from the past few years to verify employment and income history

Details on the property they intend to buy (The real estate agent can share this information.)

The paperwork is processed in much the same way as a home loan, and there may be requests for more documents.

Then, if buyers are approved, they will be ready to move ahead with a lower—or no—down payment as their homeownership journey unfolds.

Janet Siroto is a journalist, editor, and trend tracker. Her work has appeared in Cosmopolitan, Good Housekeeping, and other publications.

#5588. Dakota Fanning Cleaned Up After Sister Elle While Living and Making Their First Film Together as Co-Stars: ‘Like a Tornado Has Run Through’

Elle and Dakota Fanning have been in the spotlight for decades, but their upcoming project, “The Nightingale,” marks the first time they’ve played sisters onscreen—an experience that brought them “closer” together, both on set and at home.

While they’ve visited each other on set in the past and even separately played different versions of the same character in the 2001 film “I Am Sam,” Elle, 28, told Vanity Fair that actually working with each other is a totally different ball game.

“It certainly brought us closer, which was hard to imagine—to be closer,” she said. “Our mom always left us little notes in suitcases, like, ‘Just savor this time together. This is precious.’”

Dakota, 32, confirmed that they took their mother’s advice.

“We did really savor it,” she said. “And the biggest takeaway for me is when we have each other and when we’re together, we can do anything. That’s really how I feel. There’s nothing that I couldn’t do with Elle there with me.”

That said, the job wasn’t easy. The Fannings traveled to Budapest to shoot on location, where they lived together.

“It was a challenging shoot, not going to lie. It was physically tiring, certainly emotionally taxing,” said Elle.

After a long day of using lots of “brain power” on set, the sisters had to find a way to “recharge” each evening.

For Dakota and Elle, that meant eating lots of Thai food and streaming “The Real Housewives,” true crime, and “Margo’s Got Money Troubles”—the TV series the younger sister stars in, which was released while they filmed “The Nightingale.”

Dakota revealed that on a day off, she’d often find herself cleaning up after Elle, which was poetic as her character, Vianne, also tidies her sister Isabelle’s mess.

“Her bed in the mornings is like a tornado has run through it,” she said. “She’s just one of those sleepers. It’s all twisted into a crazy thing. I was like, ‘That’s no fun to get into a bed that’s all crumpled and rumpled. Let me make it nice.’”

The older sister said that “it became a routine,” and she “always made her bed like that” when possible.

Elle said, “It’s art imitating life, because there’s even a scene where Vianne is making Isabelle’s bed, too.”

Dakota and Elle were born in Conyers, GA. As young girls, they traveled between the Atlanta suburb and Los Angeles to work before relocating to the West Coast full time.

“When we were younger, we wanted to make sure that people saw us differently, and we wanted to give each other space to carve our own path,” Elle told Vanity Fair in 2025. “But as adults, it’s been very fulfilling to merge.”

One of the most major ways the sisters have merged their lives in adulthood was in 2017, when they purchased a gorgeous $2.3 million property together.

According to Architectural Digest, they lived in a Cape Cod-style home in the Valley Village area of San Fernando Valley.

The 4,550-square-foot residence was perched at the end of a private, gated driveway and had a very classic aesthetic with white rose bushes planted along the front walkway.

The interiors were defined by delicate details, such as baby blue brocade-patterned walls, intricate chandeliers, and coffered ceilings.

The sisters sold the six-bedroom, six-bathroom estate for just under $2.7 million in May 2020.

It’s clear that Dakota was a fan of the dwelling’s traditional style, as she bought a very similar-looking home in Toluca Lake for $2.95 million in 2019, just before offloading the property she shared with Elle.

According to Architectural Digest, Dakota’s newer home spans 4,428 square feet and boasts five bedrooms and six bathrooms. It’s flooded with natural light and, like the first home, has crystal chandeliers, a pool in the backyard, and a double-height entry hall.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5587. Enterprise AI is pushing cloud infrastructure beyond the GPU

Enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence is creating new requirements for enterprise AI infrastructure. While much of the early AI investment centered on access to powerful GPUs, organizations moving AI applications and agents into production are discovering that accelerators are only one part of the equation.

Agentic AI systems need environments where they can execute code, access data, connect to enterprise applications and operate securely across distributed infrastructure. That requires more than bare-metal GPU capacity. It calls for a complete cloud platform that combines compute, networking, storage, security and the services needed to manage applications at scale.

That shift is creating an opportunity for neocloud providers, but it is also changing what enterprises expect from them. Infrastructure providers increasingly need to support the full application lifecycle rather than simply supply specialized hardware.

During a live interview at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026, theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty spoke with Kevin Cochrane, chief marketing officer at Vultr, about the changing requirements of enterprise AI infrastructure, the return of CPU-based computing, data sovereignty and the growing role of platform engineering.

“They need a full cloud platform,” Cochrane said. “They need cloud compute, specialized AI compute, networking, storage and an open ecosystem.”

Vultr entered the cloud market in 2014 with a developer-focused platform built around performance, cost efficiency and accessibility. Since then, the company has expanded into AI infrastructure, offering both traditional cloud services and specialized GPU resources.

Cochrane said Vultr took a deliberate approach to the AI infrastructure market, prioritizing enterprise workload and platform-engineering requirements rather than focusing exclusively on GPU availability.

“We’ve always said that we’re the tortoise in AI infrastructure,” he said.

That approach reflects a broader change in how enterprises are approaching AI. Early infrastructure demand largely came from hyperscalers, AI research organizations and startups building large-scale models. Those customers needed access to GPU clusters, often through bare-metal infrastructure.

The next phase is different. Enterprises are looking to use AI agents to streamline operations, improve customer experiences and create new revenue opportunities. Those applications must work alongside existing enterprise systems, comply with security requirements and integrate with established network and application architectures.

Bare-metal GPU infrastructure alone does not address those needs. Cochrane identified complexity and a lack of specialized skills as major obstacles to enterprise AI adoption. Organizations may have access to powerful accelerators, but they still need the surrounding infrastructure and services to build, deploy and operate applications.

Vultr’s strategy is to provide a more integrated environment, including traditional cloud compute, GPU infrastructure, networking, storage and access to cloud-native projects. Cochrane said the platform supports more than 60 Cloud Native Computing Foundation projects that customers can deploy directly.

The goal is to reduce the work required to assemble an AI environment. Rather than making enterprises integrate every component themselves, providers can offer preconfigured services and composable infrastructure that developers can deploy as needed.

That distinction is becoming important as AI moves beyond experimentation. Enterprises need infrastructure that supports production applications, not just model training and inference.

The growing focus on GPUs has sometimes obscured the role of traditional computing resources in AI architectures. But agentic AI is expanding the range of workloads that infrastructure providers must support.

An AI agent does more than send a prompt to a model and receive a response. It may execute scripts, interact with repositories, run builds, access databases and invoke external tools. Those activities require compute resources beyond the GPU.

“Not all workloads need to be on a GPU,” Cochrane said.

CPUs remain essential for databases, application code and data pipelines. They can also support smaller, optimized open-source models and inference workloads that do not require dedicated accelerators.

Another emerging requirement is the environment in which agents execute tasks. As agents gain the ability to run code and interact with systems, enterprises need secure sandboxes that isolate those activities from production environments and sensitive resources.

Cochrane pointed to work underway in the cloud-native ecosystem around safe and secure agent sandboxes as an indication of how infrastructure requirements are changing.

This creates a more complex infrastructure model. GPUs may handle demanding model reasoning and inference, while CPUs support the applications, pipelines and execution environments surrounding those models.

For organizations, the implication is that enterprise AI infrastructure decisions should account for the entire agentic workflow. Buying GPU capacity without considering the compute, storage, networking and isolation requirements around it can create another infrastructure silo. A full-stack approach gives platform teams more flexibility to match resources to individual workloads while maintaining a consistent operational environment.

As enterprises expand AI deployments across regions, data sovereignty is becoming more than a question of where information is stored.

Organizations operating in regulated industries or under national data requirements need to understand where data resides, which services can access it and what happens if infrastructure outside a particular region becomes unavailable.

Cochrane described Vultr’s regional architecture as an isolation model in which each of its 34 global data center regions operates independently. According to him, data within a region remains resident there and is not accessed by Vultr services outside that region.

The distinction extends beyond data residency to application operations. Cochrane used France as an example. An application running in a French region should continue operating even if Vultr’s global control plane and its other regions become unavailable.

“If the rest of the world went dark, your production application in France? It just runs,” he said.

That approach is intended to reduce dependencies on global services that could otherwise affect regional application availability. It also gives organizations a clearer boundary for managing sensitive workloads and maintaining operational continuity.

For enterprises, this is an important architectural consideration. A cloud provider may offer regional data storage, but that does not necessarily mean every service required to operate an application is isolated within the same geography.

As AI applications become more deeply integrated into business operations, organizations will need to evaluate sovereignty across the full application stack, including data, compute, management services and operational dependencies.

The cost of running AI applications is becoming another major consideration as organizations move from pilots to sustained production workloads.

Inference costs can increase quickly when agents repeatedly call models, retrieve information and execute multi-step workflows. As usage grows, enterprises must balance model performance, throughput and infrastructure expense.

Cochrane believes some organizations will increasingly turn to open-source models that can be adapted to their own data and operated on infrastructure they control. Rather than relying entirely on large commercial models for every task, enterprises can post-train specialized models using proprietary information and deploy them for operational workloads where that approach makes sense.

He described an example involving a platform engineering organization that reduced inference costs by 80% by post-training an open-source model and running it on its own infrastructure. The example illustrates a potential economic advantage, although results will depend on the workload, model, infrastructure and operational requirements involved.

The broader point is that organizations are beginning to evaluate the economics of enterprise AI infrastructure across the entire stack. Model selection matters, but so do infrastructure utilization, throughput, data movement and the cost of operating agents over time.

For some workloads, owning more of the infrastructure and model lifecycle may provide better cost control than depending entirely on external inference services.

That does not mean every enterprise should build and operate its own models. It does suggest that organizations need more flexibility to choose where models run and how workloads are distributed.

The changing infrastructure requirements of agentic AI are also expanding the responsibilities of platform engineering teams.

Cochrane expects platform engineers to become central to enterprise AI adoption, working more closely with business units to understand which agents and preconfigured application environments are needed across the organization.

That moves platform engineering beyond infrastructure provisioning and developer enablement. Teams will increasingly need to help define the building blocks that allow developers to deploy governed AI applications without having to assemble every component independently.

Cochrane also sees an opportunity for the cloud-native community to evolve how it shares infrastructure patterns. The CNCF ecosystem has helped developers adopt individual open-source projects across networking, storage, observability and other infrastructure categories. But as architectures become more complex, organizations need guidance on how those components fit together.

Cochrane predicted the emergence of marketplaces where developers can share opinionated, prebuilt stacks for specific workload types. Instead of selecting and configuring individual components, teams could start with a tested architecture and adapt it to their requirements. That could help reduce the complexity of building agentic applications while encouraging more consistent deployment practices.

He also expects consolidation in the neocloud market. Providers focused primarily on bare-metal GPU capacity may face pressure as enterprises demand broader cloud capabilities. Those able to expand into full public cloud platforms could be better positioned to serve production workloads.

Vultr’s existing cloud platform gives it a foundation for that transition, Cochrane said, with its investments in both traditional compute and specialized AI infrastructure.

Enterprise AI is changing the definition of cloud infrastructure. GPUs remain important, but agentic applications require a broader foundation that includes CPUs, secure execution environments, networking, storage, data sovereignty and integrated cloud-native services.

That creates an opportunity for providers that can deliver more than specialized accelerator capacity. It also puts platform engineering teams in a more strategic position as enterprises work to standardize how AI applications are built, deployed and governed.

The next phase of the neocloud market may therefore be determined less by who can offer the most GPU capacity and more by who can provide the complete environment enterprises need to run AI in production.

As Cochrane’s comments suggest, the infrastructure challenge is no longer simply making AI compute available. It is making the entire system around AI practical to operate at enterprise scale.

#5586. Angie Katsanevas Reveals Estranged Husband Shawn Trujillo Bought a New $1.1 Million Home Near Family’s Modern Utah Mansion: ‘We Are Not Reconciling’

Four months after announcing their split, “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City” cast member Angie Katsanevas and her estranged husband, Shawn Trujillo, are now living in separate homes.

“Recently, Shawn has bought a place that’s two minutes down the street. And I’m at home with Elektra,” Katsanevas revealed in a new People magazine interview.

According to a Page Six report, Trujillo's new pad is a $1.1 million condo he purchased in September. The two-story dwelling spans 2,568 square feet and includes three bedrooms and 4.5 bathrooms.

The couple, who married in June 1999, have yet to legally divorce, but are "moving toward" that status.

“We are separated. We haven’t put it on paper, but we are not reconciling as far as staying married,” the reality TV star, 53, explained. “I hate the big D-word, but I’ll just have to say that, yeah, we are moving toward the big D.”

The salon owner’s home—which viewers will recognize from the reality series—is a sprawling hillside estate that has been on and off the market for the past two years.

The four-bedroom, three-bathroom modern abode was first listed for $4.5 million in September 2024. The price was decreased to $4.38 million in March 2025, then to $3.85 million just two months later.

By December of last year, the listing was removed. It hit the market again in January 2026 for $3.85 million, where it sat for most of the year before being removed on Oct. 14.

The couple purchased the 6,369-square-foot residence for an undisclosed sum in 2020. With soaring ceilings, white ash floors, and lots of sleek, marble surfaces, the modern abode has a distinct luxurious aesthetic.

The home has two primary suites, with one that includes a fireplace, sitting area, and double-vanity bathroom with a striking view of the surrounding Utah landscape. There are also dual walk-in closets.

The second is located on the main floor and also has two-walk in closets and a gorgeous bathroom.

Features in pairs seem to be a feature of the home in general, as there are also two kitchens. In addition to the chic white minimalist space at the center of the home, a concealed catering kitchen is equipped with Miele appliances, a separate refrigerator and freezer, and a space for staff to prepare food.

It seems as if, despite the separation, daily life hasn’t changed too much in the home. Katsanevas noted that Trujillo stops by most days to pick up their 15-year-old daughter, Elektra, and take her to school.

“He’ll come in and have coffee,” she explained. “He’ll bring her home from lessons, and we’ll have dinner together. We are still just spending time together. We’re best friends. We are peaceful, it’s positive. We have a lot to do together.”

She noted that Trujillo remains close with her father and will celebrate the holidays with the family.

“My dad sends him all of his favorite dishes and continues to cook for him,” said Katsanevas. “Shawn will spend Thanksgiving and Christmas with my family.”

Although they are still connected in many ways, Katsanevas noted that after nearly three decades together, “space and doing things independently” have brought clarity.

“We are even going to different churches now,” she shared. “And that’s huge for me. We started out going to the same church.”

Katsanevas also shut down rumors that she had initiated the split over their opposing political stances, a rumor that started after she cited their “different views” in a confessional interview during a recent episode of “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City.”

“I’m not throwing a 30-year marriage away because of rumors or political views,” she said. “There are so many things that Shawn and I have grown apart and have different views on, a lot of things at this stage of life. And it’s not one thing. It’s just, we’re very different people.”

They’re still business partners, however, and are set to open a new hair salon together in Miami.

“We are continuing to grow our brand together, even though we are separated,” she said.

Katsanevas and Trujillo currently operate nine locations of their business, Lunatic Fringe Salon, across Utah, Ohio, and Idaho.

While she’s focused on remaining positive, Katsanevas said it took some time to work through the complicated feelings that accompanied the change.

“It does take a minute to mourn the loss of the way your life once was and what it looked like,” she said. “I’ve processed, I’ve cried, I’ve accepted. I’ve had to swim away from the muddy waters to get to the clear water and say, ‘OK, I’m coming out of this and I’m going to be OK.’”

#5585. Medical AI startup Boltz raises $110M to speed up small molecule research

Boltz PBC, a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for pharmaceutical researchers, has raised $110 million in funding.

Bessemer led the Series A investment. Boltz stated on Wednesday that the fund was joined by a large group of new and returning backers. The consortium included Greycroft, Andreessen Horowitz, Amplify Partners, F-Prime Capital, Hummingbird and others.

Small molecules, the building blocks of many drugs, can only neutralize a pathogen after binding to it. As a result, researchers start drug discovery projects by looking for molecules that have a high binding affinity with pathogens. They often review hundreds of thousands of candidate molecules per project. The process can take months and often costs millions of dollars.

Boltz offers an AI model called BoltzMol-1 that speeds up the workflow. It generates binding affinity data by reviewing only a few dozen, particularly promising molecules instead of the hundreds of thousands usually needed. The fewer molecules need to be studied, the less time the analysis takes.

Binding affinity evaluations don’t yield drug discoveries right away. Instead, they produce data points called small molecule hits. Those are essentially faint clues that help researchers pinpoint the area where they should focus their efforts.

Boltz staffers asked BoltzMol-1 to look for small molecule hits across 10 “challenging and therapeutically-relevant targets.” Targets are biological building blocks that play a role in disease processes. According to the company, the model found small molecule hits for six of the targets.

Scientists can adapt BoltzMol-1 to project-specific constraints. If a research team has access to a relatively limited number of compounds, it could configure the model to only consider small molecules that can be made from those compounds. When material procurement is not an obstacle, BoltzMol-1 evaluates a much larger number of candidates.

The company also offers a second model called BoltzProt-1. It can generate tens of thousands of protein designs based on data gleaned from small molecule hits. Additionally, BoltzProt-1 automatically reviews each protein to determine if it could be used to develop a new drug.

Usually, AI models evaluate protein designs based on rubrics that provide only an indirect view of their effectiveness. BoltzProt-1 uses more direct metrics. The company says that BoltzProt-1’s protein evaluation mechanism demonstrated “higher success” than several competing models during internal tests.

Boltz sells its algorithms via an application programming interface that is billed based on token usage. According to the company, customers’ token consumption has grown by a factor of 50 since BoltzMol-1 and BoltzProt-1 launched in June. Boltz counts six of the world’s 20 largest pharmaceutical companies as clients.

The company will use its new funding to grow its headcount and procure more computing infrastructure. #5584. Anthropic’s $1.5 Trillion Valuation Exceeds the Worth of Every Home in San Francisco

Anthropic’s initial public offering priced above expectations for its IPO on Thursday, with the company’s fully diluted valuation coming to roughly $1.494 trillion—more than the total residential real estate values in many entire states.

The Claude developer, which will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, priced at $83 a share, above the predicted $70 to $78 range. The company sold 980 million Class A shares, raising an initial $81 billion and shattering SpaceX’s $72 billion record.

To help better understand the massive $1.494 trillion price tag, Realtor.com® put the number in terms of real estate—and the statistics are shocking.

San Francisco is a longtime hot spot for tech giants. It saw the growth of Google and Facebook, and has now become the landing spot for Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI startups. The constant stream of tech wealth, combined with a limited number of desirable homes, has created a competitive market. San Francisco County has a median sales price of $1.6 million, and yet, Anthropic blows the entire market out of the water.

The aggregate value of every home for sale in San Francisco is a mere $8.6 billion, a small fraction of Anthropic's new valuation. Indeed, the total value of every owner-occupied home in the San Francisco metro is $1.37 trillion, according to the 2-25 American Community Survey. Anthropic’s valuation exceeds that by about $123 billion.

This trend is consistent in 391 metros out of 393.

The only two metros with more owner-occupied home value than Anthropic is worth are New York City, at $3.26 trillion, and Los Angeles, at $2.64 trillion.

Furthermore, the AI giant’s valuation tops the owner-occupied home value in 46 out of the 50 states, as well as Washington, DC.

The value of all owner-occupied homes in the state of New Jersey comes in at $1.44 trillion, just shy of Anthropic’s valuation.

Throughout the country, all owner-occupied homes are worth $43.6 trillion. Anthropic’s valuation equals about 3.4% of all owner-occupied housing wealth in the United States.

When it comes to homes on the market, Anthropic’s valuation stacks up high.

Across the U.S., about 1.18 million homes are for sale, listed for a combined $816 billion. Anthropic’s valuation could snap up every single one and still have $678 billion left.

Even without the first $1 trillion of the valuation, the remaining $494 billion could buy every home for sale in the 20 metros with the highest total listing value with billions to spare: about 372,000 homes listed at a combined $356 billion.

As Anthropic’s debut is discussed, the valuation may be rounded to $1.49 trillion, as it’s common for financial figures to be kept to one or two digits. However, that dropped digit in the $1.494 trillion figure is $4 billion. That rounding error alone is greater than the combined value of every owner-occupied home in Racine, WI, which total $3.97 billion.

That same $4 billion could buy every home for sale in Alaska: 2,196 listings worth $1.16 billion. For a change in scenery, it could then cover every home for sale on Kauai, the Kapa’a, Hawaii, market, which has 356 listings worth $925 million, and still have about $1.9 billion left to purchase all the homes for sale in the Boulder, CO, metro area.

It’s no wonder the AI boom is reshaping markets in tech hubs like New York City and San Francisco, when the valuation of just one company looms so high.

#5583. Selling Your Home? What You Should Know About Price Cuts vs. Rate Buydowns.

In today’s market, a growing number of sellers are opting to do something called a price cut – especially when their house has been on the market for a while without any bites.

According to HousingWire Data as many as 4 in 10 (43%) sellers are going this route – that’s the highest it’s been in 4 years. But what if there’s another (potentially better option) for your bottom line? And it’s just as appealing, if not more so, to today’s buyers?

First, let’s set the stage on why some compromise may be necessary in today’s market.

In September, Redfin says there were 63% more sellers than buyers in the market. And with so many sellers active and relatively few buyers by comparison, those purchasers are realizing they have more power. And as mortgage rates continue to put a squeeze on their budgets, they’re leaning in and using it.

One of the most common negotiation points? The price.

That’s because they want to feel like they’re getting a deal and they want to see their monthly payment drop. And since buyers can’t control rates, the price feels like the most obvious lever to pull.

But the savviest sellers realize being flexible doesn’t always mean a lower price, paying for a buyer’s rate buydown might work better.

A buydown is money paid at closing to lower the buyer’s mortgage rate. When you pay it as the seller, you are paying some of the buyer’s interest ahead of time, so the buyer gets a lower rate and monthly payment. And that’s especially appealing to today’s buyers.

Temporary buydowns lower the rate for the first few years, then it goes back to the full rate. The more years a buydown covers, the more it costs. These work well for buyers who expect to refinance within a certain amount of time.

A permanent buydown lowers the rate for the whole loan. These are paid for with “discount points.” One point costs 1% of the loan. According to FICO, each point generally lowers the rate by about a quarter of a percent. This type of buydown works well for buyers who plan to stay in the home for a long time.

And here’s why these can be a win-win for both buyers and sellers. Rate buydowns help sellers stand out in a crowded market and they can have a bigger impact on your buyer than a price cut would.

Here’s an example to show you what that could look like.

Let’s say you’re willing to make a $10,000 concession to help get the deal done. Take a look at these three ways to spend that money and the impact they could have on a buyer’s $420,000, 30-year fixed loan at 7%:

It’s the same $10,000 from the seller. But a 2-1 buydown saves the buyer about eight times more each month in the first year.

And since most buyers shop by monthly payment, that’s what grabs their attention.

That’s what makes a rate buydown worth considering. Instead of reducing your asking price, you may be able to use that same money to have a bigger impact on your buyer’s monthly payments. And depending on what matters most to that buyer, the immediate savings could be more appealing than a price reduction.

The key is working with your agent and the buyer’s lender to compare the options and see which one makes the most sense.

Loan programs cap how much a seller can pay toward a buyer’s costs.

Money toward buydowns doesn’t limit what else a buyer may ask a seller to pay for. Buyers may still ask for repairs or other concessions.

Putting the buydown offer in your listing lets agents and buyers know it’s an option.

Your agent can run scenarios on buydowns and other costs of selling in advance so you’re prepared when an offer comes in.

As Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), says:

“Home sellers need to be realistic about local market conditions, which could require price discounts and other incentives to attract buyers.”

And sellers who offer solutions like buydowns can make meaningful impact where home buyers need it most: in their wallets.

When you're looking for ways to make your house more appealing to buyers, a price reduction isn't your only option. A mortgage rate buydown could help a buyer save more each month, especially in the early years of their loan.Talk to your agent or a trusted lender which incentives could make the biggest difference for buyers in our market, while still protecting your bottom line.
